title: First Sunday of Lent
hook: the gospel is always the temptation in the desert
tomorrow: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday: dust, and Joel's line, rend your hearts. Is your quiet sacrifice still a secret? Day six hundred fifty-two.

The Sunday readings change on a three-year cycle. Matthew one year, Mark the next, Luke the third. Most of the gospels change from one year to the next. But on the first Sunday of Lent, whichever year it is, whichever gospel, the story is the same: Jesus, alone in the wilderness, hungry, and tempted. The Church has fixed it there like a signpost at the trailhead. Before you walk the forty days, here's who walked them first, and how it went.
screen: `A THREE-YEAR CYCLE.` → `ONE STORY THAT NEVER MOVES.` → `A SIGNPOST AT THE TRAILHEAD.`

segments.voice: Right after his baptism, the voice from heaven still ringing, the Spirit leads Jesus into the desert. He fasts forty days and forty nights, and afterward, the text says simply, he was hungry. Forty is not a random number. Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness. Moses stayed forty days on the mountain. Elijah walked forty days to the mountain of God. Jesus steps into the same desert his people knew. Then the tempter comes, three times. First, the hungry man: if thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. He answers from Deuteronomy, in the Douay-Rheims: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." Second, on the pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. Third, on a high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world, his for one act of worship. Each time he answers with a line from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's own desert years. Three temptations, people have noticed, that touch almost everyone: comfort, attention, and power. Mark tells the whole thing in two verses, and adds a detail no other Gospel has: he was with the wild beasts, and the angels ministered to him. On this Sunday, in many dioceses, adults preparing for baptism at Easter are presented to the bishop and enrolled, the Rite of Election. Their forty days begin with his. Lent, in Latin, is Quadragesima, the fortieth. The whole season is shaped like this desert.
screen: `LED INTO THE DESERT.` · `FORTY, THE OLD NUMBER.` · `BREAD, A LEAP, THE KINGDOMS.` · `COMFORT, ATTENTION, POWER.` · then, large: `NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your desert. Sit, and let it get quiet. Ask what your wilderness is right now: a loneliness, a waiting, a craving, a fear, a stretch of life where things feel empty. Name it plainly, in one word if you can. Then ask which of the three pulls at you hardest there: comfort, attention, or power. No judging. Just naming. If you pray, you can ask for the angels Mark mentions, to minister to you. If you don't, simply stay with what you named. The bell holds the time.
Quadragesima, the fortieth. The Church's Latin name for Lent, the forty days that begin each year with Jesus tempted in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. Today, when one of the three pulls at you, comfort, attention or power, notice it and name it. Day six hundred fifty-two.

fork.setup: you've fasted forty days and you're starving. a voice says: if you're the Son of God, turn these stones into bread. what do you say?
options: make the bread; there's no harm in eating.
not in bread alone doth man live.
fork.reveal: he answers from Deuteronomy 8:3: not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word from the mouth of God.

original.note: Latin: the fortieth (day), the Church's Latin name for Lent.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lent is forty days of giving up chocolate.
what it means: forty days shaped like Jesus's desert, opened every year by the temptation gospel.
what a scholar hears: every answer quotes Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:16, 6:13), so Jesus relives Israel's forty desert years, answering with the lessons of that same desert.

notes: 'Comfort, attention, and power' is a common homiletic reading of the three temptations, presented as 'people have noticed'. Confirm.

Trapdoor originally said Jesus 'passes where they struggled'; softened in review to 'answering with the lessons of that same desert' to avoid an unfavorable contrast with Israel. Typological reading; confirm.
Rite of Election usually celebrated on or near the First Sunday of Lent. Confirm.
Quadragesima pronunciation given in ecclesiastical Latin; confirm.
Audit (second sample): 'almost nothing repeats' overstated the three-year cycle (softened); the stock 'strange, lovely detail' now says what is distinctive: only Mark mentions the wild beasts.
